rationale: The amount of expression signal differs a lot between drugs: cytotoxic and targeted oncology drugs carry strong signal, while many repurposed non-oncology drugs carry almost none. A single shared ridge penalty (alpha=5000) is therefore a poor compromise. I keep the same features but let each drug pick its own ridge penalty by efficient leave-one-out cross-validation on the training fold. This is cheap and data-driven: drugs with strong signal get light shrinkage and noisy drugs get heavy shrinkage.

Drug responses in PRISM share a few strong axes (overall cell-line sensitivity and MOA clusters), while each drug's own residual is mostly noise. So I'm replacing the mean-filled targets with a low-rank version of the drug × line AUC matrix. Missing values are filled by iterative SVD, and the rank is chosen by grouped inner CV on the training fold. This is reduced-rank multi-task ridge: drugs with weak signal can borrow strength from related drugs. Expression features and the ridge penalty stay the same as the current best.

Much of PRISM drug sensitivity follows tissue lineage. A ridge model on 5,000 genes under heavy shrinkage (alpha=5000) only recovers lineage indirectly and weakly. So I add one-hot OncotreeLineage indicators next to the standardized genes. Their scale sets how lightly lineage is penalized, and I pick it from {0, 3, 10, 30} by grouped inner CV on the training fold. Scale 0 reproduces the current model exactly, so inner CV can fall back to it.

I'm blending the current linear ridge with an RBF kernel ridge on the same standardized top-variance genes. The RBF kernel captures nonlinear "similar cell lines respond similarly" structure, such as lineage and transcriptional state, that a heavily shrunk linear model misses. The blend weight and kernel penalty are chosen by grouped inner CV on mean per-drug Pearson, and a weight of 0 gives back the current model exactly.

For many drugs in PRISM, sensitivity depends on a few sharp marker genes (for example ABCB1 efflux, SLFN11 or the drug's target pathway). A heavily shrunk ridge on 5,000 variance-selected genes spreads its weight too thinly to use them. I add a per-drug model that first picks, inside the training fold, the genes most correlated with that drug's AUC, then fits a ridge on them. It is blended with the current shared ridge. The number of genes, the penalty and the blend weight are chosen by grouped inner CV on mean per-drug Pearson, and a weight of 0 gives back the current model exactly.

With about 380 training lines, each drug's gene-AUC correlations are noisy, so the per-drug screen often picks spurious genes. Drugs that share an MOA or most of their targets (for example HDAC, MEK, tubulin or proteasome inhibitors) should have the same marker genes. So I screen each drug's genes on its correlation vector smoothed with the average correlation vector of its MOA/target neighbours. The smoothing strength γ∈{0,1} is added to the grouped inner-CV grid, and γ=0 gives back the current model exactly.

The per-drug model currently uses a hard top-k screen, so the 3rd marker gene and the 1000th count equally. I'm adding a soft version: within the top 1,000 screened genes, each gene column is scaled by its relative screening correlation raised to a power p (p ∈ {1, 2}). That acts as a gene-specific ridge prior, so strong markers like ABCB1, SLFN11 or target-pathway genes get less shrinkage while weaker genes still add a little. p is added to the grouped inner-CV grid next to the existing hard screens, so inner CV can still fall back to the current model. I haven't run this; I estimate the extra fits raise runtime by about two thirds, to roughly 13 minutes against the ~25-minute limit.

Right now one (screen, λ, γ, blend-weight) setting is chosen for all 200 drugs. Drugs differ a lot in how much marker-gene signal they carry: targeted and cytotoxic drugs benefit from the per-drug screen, while noisy repurposed drugs do better leaning on the shared ridge. So I now choose the setting per drug, shrunk toward the global choice: score = (1−s)·r_drug + s·r_mean. Both the shrinkage s and the option set (blend weight only, or the full setting) are picked by cross-fitting across the existing inner grouped folds: choose on two folds, score on the third. This needs no extra model fits, and s=1 gives back the current model exactly.

With about 380 training lines, each drug's gene–AUC correlations are noisy. Genes that really drive response tend to sit in connected STRING modules (target pathway, efflux, apoptosis). So I'm adding a third screening variant: each drug's correlation vector is averaged with the mean correlation of each gene's STRING neighbours (score ≥ 700) before genes are screened. This is network propagation of the screen. I'm also switching the hard screens with fewer genes than lines (k < n) to the equivalent primal ridge. Existing configs give the same predictions, and the third variant should stay inside the time budget. The variant enters the same per-drug, cross-fitted option selection, so drugs can still fall back to the raw or MOA-smoothed screens. I haven't run this, so the score and runtime are untested.

I'm adding sharing between related drugs at the prediction level. After each drug's blend is chosen, its z-scored test prediction is mixed with the mean prediction of its neighbour drugs: (1−η)·z_j + η·mean_nb(z). Neighbours are defined either by shared MOA/targets or by strong AUC correlation in the training fold (r ≥ 0.5, top 10). Drugs in one pharmacological class (tubulin, HDAC, MEK, proteasome inhibitors and so on) respond to the same biology, and their per-drug models are fitted on different noisy labels. Averaging their predictions should therefore cut variance more than smoothing the gene screen alone. The neighbour type and η ∈ {0, 0.15, 0.3, 0.5} are chosen by cross-fitting over the existing inner grouped folds, and η=0 gives back the current model exactly. I haven't run this, so the score is untested; the extra cost is small because it adds no new model fits.

I'm adding pathway-level features as an option for each drug. A pathway score is the mean of the training-standardized gene z-scores across a Hallmark or Reactome set (15–300 genes). On top of the gene screens, I add a screened ridge on the top 25 or top 100 pathway scores most correlated with each drug, with optional MOA-neighbour smoothing. Averaging over a pathway should be much less noisy than single genes for drugs driven by broad cell states such as proliferation, EMT, interferon, OXPHOS or the apoptosis machinery. These pathway screens enter the same per-drug selection and blend-weight choice used for the gene screens, so a drug keeps its current setting unless the pathway screen scores better on the training fold's inner folds. Pathway fits are small and cheap, so the extra runtime is modest. I haven't run this, so the score and runtime are untested.
